newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU calls for Israeli moves to restart peace.
newsitem.headline: EU calls for Israeli moves to restart peace.

text.p: The European Union, rolling out its toughest language to date on the subject, rebuked Israel on Tuesday for failing to meet its obligations in the Middle East peace process.

In a statement coinciding with the start of a summit in Washington on the deteriorating situation between Israelis and Palestinians, EU foreign ministers, meeting in Luxembourg, expressed clear frustration with Israel's new government.

Calling on restraint from both sides, the ministers said Israel should reconsider its opening of a controversial archaeological tunnel under Jerusalem's old town, reopen the borders with the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, and withdraw from Hebron.
"(The European Union) calls on Israel to match its stated commitment to the peace process with complete actions to fulfil its obligations," a statement said.

In a particularly pointed snub, the EU also reaffirmed its position that East Jerusalem was "not under Israeli sovereignty". One EU diplomat said this was the first time the bloc had publicly put this on paper.

EU officials said the ministers had agreed what they believed to be a balanced position reflecting the current state of affairs in the region, including calling on the Palestinian Authority to control its forces.
"You may say it is unbalanced, but that is where the situation is," the diplomat said.

The statement said the 15-member EU hoped the Washington summit would lead to the re-starting of constructive negotiations. It also called for an end to the recent violence in which at least 72 people have been killed.
"(We urge) both sides to avoid resorting to disproportionate force, in particular the use of firearms, tanks and helicopter gunships," the statement said.
Although the ministers said they were not apportioning blame at any side in particular, it was clear from the tone that Israeli actions were seen as the catalyst for the troubles.
"In our judgment it is up to the Israeli government to demonstrate what they might do to help the process," British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said.

"It is clear that the basic problem is that the new government is violating the Oslo agreement (on Middle East Peace) while the Palestinian side fulfils its part," Swedish Foreign Aid Minister Pierre Schori told reporters.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said he had personally urged his colleagues not to load too much blame on Israel.
"I urged them not to put Israel in the stocks," he said. "But our concern about the situation had to be expressed."
The EU call came as the United States was hosting a summit between Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and King Hussein of Jordan in Washington.

The summit was called by U.S. President Bill Clinton to try to salvage the peace process threatened by an outbreak of unrest touched off when Israel opened a new exit for the tunnel under Temple Mount in Jerusalem, a site holy to both Jews and Moslems.

Earlier, the EU ministers had pledged to continue financial support for the West Bank and Gaza Strip, and approved plans to include the fledgling Palestinian entity in a lucrative Mediterrannean trade bloc.
